n16-1.name: Priam’s Birdwing
facts: The first birdwing ever described, named by Linnaeus in 1758 after Priam, king of Troy. He gave the great swallowtails the names of Trojan heroes.
The male’s green is structural colour, not pigment: microscopic ridges on the scales scatter light. The engraver could only approximate it with paint.
Females are larger, brown and cream, and were long thought to be a different species.
Caterpillars feed on poisonous Dutchman’s pipe vines and carry the toxin into adulthood, so birds learn to leave the adults alone.
n16-1.range: Moluccas to New Guinea and northern Australia
n16-1.caption: g. Ornithoptera Priamus ♂, île d’Amboine

n18-1.name: Golden Birdwing
facts: Troides rhadamantus, the tropical golden birdwing, is a birdwing butterfly that inhabits the Philippines. The species was first described by Hippolyte Lucas in 1835.
Lucas called it Ornithoptera rhadamantus; the accepted name today is Troides rhadamantus.

n18-2.name: Androgeus Swallowtail
facts: Papilio androgeus, the Androgeus swallowtail, queen page, or queen swallowtail, is a Neotropical butterfly of the family Papilionidae. It is found from Mexico to Argentina with a small population in southern Florida.
Lucas called it Papilio polycaon; the accepted name today is Papilio androgeus.

n20-1.name: Ulysses Butterfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are velvet black above, with a patch of azure blue that turns violet or green according to the angle at which one examines it. This patch runs from the base of all four wings to beyond the middle, its hind edge scalloped, and near the front edge of the forewings there is a fairly large black dot, present in the female too.”

Papilio ulysses, the Ulysses butterfly, is a large swallowtail butterfly, in the subgenus Achillides, of Australia, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. Its size varies depending on subspecies, but the wingspan is about 10.5 cm (4.1 in) in Queensland.
Parides agavus, the Agavus Cattleheart, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is found in Brazil, Paraguay, and north Argentina.
Lucas called it Papilio agavus; the accepted name today is Parides agavus.

n22-2.name: Common Mormon
facts: Papilio polytes, the common Mormon, is a common species of swallowtail butterfly widely distributed across Asia.

n32-1.name: Blue Triangle
facts: Graphium sarpedon, the common bluebottle is a species of swallowtail butterfly that is found in East, South and Southeast Asia. There are approximately sixteen subspecies with differing geographical distributions.
Lucas called it Papilio sarpedon; the accepted name today is Graphium sarpedon.

n32-2.name: Veined Jay
facts: Graphium bathycles, the veined jay, is a butterfly in the family Papilionidae, that is found in the Indomalayan realm.

n34-1.name: Great Emesis
facts: Lucas called it Papilio polymetus; the accepted name today is Emesis mandana.

n34-2.name: Common Clubtail
facts: Losaria coon, the common clubtail, is a butterfly belonging to the swallowtail family, Papilionidae. The butterfly belongs to the clubtails, genus Losaria.
Lucas called it Papilio coon; the accepted name today is Losaria coon.
Mylon maimon, the common mylon or black-veined mylon, is a butterfly of the family Hesperiidae. It is found from Argentina to Colombia and Bolivia, and north to Mexico.

n36-2.name: Vertumnus Cattleheart
facts: Parides vertumnus  is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is found in the Neotropical realm.
Lucas called it Papilio vertumnus; the accepted name today is Parides vertumnus.

n38-1.name: Chocolate Pansy
facts: Junonia iphita, the chocolate pansy or chocolate soldier, is a butterfly found in Asia.
Lucas called it Papilio iphitas; the accepted name today is Junonia iphita.

n38-2.name: Pipevine Swallowtail
facts: Battus philenor, the pipevine swallowtail or blue swallowtail, is a swallowtail butterfly found in North America and Central America. This butterfly is black with iridescent-blue hindwings.
Lucas called it Papilio philenor; the accepted name today is Battus philenor.

n40-1.name: Lucerne Butterfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are toothed, black, with whitish notches. The forewings carry a whitish, interrupted streak opposite the apex; the hindwings are crossed in the middle by a broad greyish-white band, sinuous on its outer side, ending at the anal angle in a blood-red lunule dusted with blue.”
Colias electo, the African clouded yellow or lucerne butterfly, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found in eastern and southern Africa, as well as Arabia.
Lucas called it Papilio erecteus; the accepted name today is Colias electo.

n40-2.name: Citrus Swallowtail
facts: Papilio demoleus is a common and widespread swallowtail butterfly. The butterfly is also known as the lemon butterfly and chequered swallowtail.

n50-1.name: Small Reunion Swallowtail
facts: Papilio phorbanta, also known as the small Réunion swallowtail, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is thought to be endemic to Réunion but may also be present on the Seychelles, but it might be extinct there.

n50-2.name: Small Reunion Swallowtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are toothed, of a deep blackish brown above, with whitish notches. Towards the middle of the wing the male shows a large patch of fine blue-green, set transversely and divided in three by the veins, and near the apex of the same wings three more spots of the same colour.”

Papilio phorbanta, also known as the small Réunion swallowtail, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is thought to be endemic to Réunion but may also be present on the Seychelles, but it might be extinct there.
Lucas called it Papilio disparilis; the accepted name today is Papilio phorbanta.

n52-1.name: Scarlet Mormon Swallowtail
facts: Papilio deiphobus is a species of swallowtail butterfly in the Papilioninae subfamily. It is found from the Mollucas to Sulawesi in Indonesia.

n54-1.name: Blue Mormon
facts: Papilio agenor polymnestor, the Indian blue mormon, is a large swallowtail butterfly found in south India. It is the "state butterfly" of the Indian state of Maharashtra.

n54-2.name: Swift Peacock Swallowtail
facts: Papilio peranthus, the Indonesian swallowtail is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae. It is found in Indonesia.

n56-1.name: Giant Swallowtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “This species, of middling size, is sulphur white on both surfaces. The tip of the forewings is edged above by a broad arched black band, much widened at the apex, where it carries a dot of the ground colour; the hindwings have very blunt teeth and a fairly long yellowish spatulate tail, with three black spots towards the middle of the surface.”

The eastern giant swallowtail is the largest butterfly in North America. It is abundant through many parts of eastern North America; populations from western North America and down into Panama are now considered to belong to a different species, Papilio rumiko.

n56-2.name: Red Helen
facts: Papilio helenus, the red Helen, is a large swallowtail butterfly found in forests of southern India and parts of southeast Asia.

n66-1.name: White-barred Charaxes
facts: Charaxes brutus, the white-barred emperor or white-barred Charaxes, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Africa.
Lucas called it Papilio brutus; the accepted name today is Charaxes brutus.

n66-2.name: Mocker Swallowtail
facts: Papilio dardanus, the Saharan swallowtail, African swallowtail, mocker swallowtail or flying handkerchief, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. The species is broadly distributed throughout Sub-Saharan Africa.
Parides aeneas is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is found in the Neotropical realm.
Lucas called it Papilio aeneas; the accepted name today is Parides aeneas.

n68-1.name: Southern Cattle Heart
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are deep black above and crossed towards the middle by a band of greenish yellow, narrowed and broken into round spots near the apex of the forewings; the hindwings carry a row of lunules of the same colour parallel to the hind edge. These wings are very bluntly toothed, edged with white at the notches, and end in a black tail a little spatulate.”
Parides sesostris, the emerald-patched cattleheart or southern cattleheart, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae.
Lucas called it Papilio sesostris; the accepted name today is Parides sesostris.

n68-2.name: Green-underside Blue
facts: Glaucopsyche alexis, the green-underside blue, is a butterfly of the family Lycaenidae. It is found in the Palearctic.
Lucas called it Papilio dimas; the accepted name today is Glaucopsyche alexis.

n70-1.name: Fluminense Swallowtail
facts: Parides ascanius, the Fluminense swallowtail, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is endemic to Brazil where it is confined to the municipalities of Atafona and Itaguaí.It is found in subcoastal swamps and thickets ('restinga').

Eurema brigitta, the small grass yellow or broad-bordered grass yellow, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites. It is found in India, other parts of Asia, Australia and Africa.

n80-1.name: Belus Swallowtail
facts: Battus belus, the Belus swallowtail is a species of butterfly from the family Papilionidae that is found in Brazil, Colombia, Guatemala, Peru and Venezuela.
Lucas called it Papilio belus; the accepted name today is Battus belus.

n80-2.name: Polydamas Swallowtail
facts: Battus polydamas, also known as the gold rim swallowtail, the Polydamas swallowtail or the tailless swallowtail, is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. The species was first described by Carl Linnaeus in his 10th edition of Systema Naturae, published in 1758.
Lucas called it Papilio polydamas; the accepted name today is Battus polydamas.

n82-1.name: Victorine Swallowtail
facts: Papilio menatius is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae.
Lucas called it Papilio licoraeus; the accepted name today is Papilio menatius.

n82-2.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
facts: Papilio glaucus, the eastern tiger swallowtail, is a species of butterfly native to eastern North America. It is one of the most familiar butterflies in the eastern United States, ranging north to southern Ontario, Canada, and is common in many different habitats.
Lucas called it Papilio turnus; the accepted name today is Papilio glaucus.

n84-1.name: Chinese Swallowtail
facts: Papilio xuthus, the Asian swallowtail, Chinese yellow swallowtail, Japanese swallowtail, Korean swallowtail or Xuthus swallowtail, is a yellow-colored, medium to large sized swallowtail butterfly found in northeast Asia, northern Myanmar, southern China, Taiwan, the Korean Peninsula, Japan, Siberia…

n84-2.name: Spicebush Swallowtail
facts: Papilio troilus, the spicebush swallowtail or green-clouded butterfly, is a common black swallowtail butterfly found in North America. It has two subspecies, Papilio troilus troilus and Papilio troilus ilioneus, the latter found mainly in the Florida peninsula.

n86-1.name: Peacock Pansy
facts: Lucas, 1835: “This species of middling size is brownish black, with a yellow transverse band made up of triangular spots on the forewings and divided by black veins on the hindwings. The hind edge of the forewings is slightly toothed and preceded by a row of yellow dots; the hindwings have curved blunt teeth, a black tail of moderate length, and a tawny anal angle marked with a very black dot beneath a lunule of blue atoms.”

Junonia almana, the peacock pansy, is a species of nymphalid butterfly found in Cambodia and South Asia. It exists in two distinct adult forms, which differ chiefly in the patterns on the underside of the wings; the dry-season form has few markings, while the wet-season form has additional eyespots…
Lucas called it Papilio asterias; the accepted name today is Junonia almana.

n86-2.name: Cream-lined Swallowtail
facts: Papilio delalandei is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae. It is endemic to Madagascar.
Protesilaus protesilaus is a species of butterfly of the family Papilionidae. It is found in the Neotropical realm.
Lucas called it Papilio protesilaus; the accepted name today is Protesilaus protesilaus.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above with a very faint greenish tint, gently strengthened at the base and apex of the forewings; along the costa run seven transverse black bands, the three foremost nearly equal, the next two short, the two hindmost longer and broader, ending in a point and meeting near the inner angle. The hindwings have their lower edge cut by black lunules, mostly on an ashen ground.”
Mimoides lysithous  is a species of butterfly in the family Papilionidae. It is found in the Neotropical realm.
Lucas called it Papilio pompilius; the accepted name today is Mimoides lysithous.

n98-2.name: Black Swallowtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above, with an interrupted band, four transverse streaks and a row of marginal spots of pale green. The band curves inward and crosses the middle of all four wings; the streak nearest the body continues on the hindwings to above the anal angle, where it ends in a dot of carmine red.”

Papilio polyxenes, the (eastern) black swallowtail, American swallowtail or parsnip swallowtail, is a butterfly found throughout much of North America. An extremely similar-appearing species, Papilio joanae, occurs in the Ozark Mountains region, but it appears to be closely related to Papilio…

n100-1.name: Lesser Zebra
facts: Graphium macareus, the lesser zebra, is a relatively common and not threatened species of swallowtail butterfly found in Southeast Asia. It is also found in parts of India including Assam and Sikkim.
Lucas called it Papilio macareus; the accepted name today is Graphium macareus.

n100-2.name: Common Mime
facts: Papilio clytia, the common mime, is a swallowtail butterfly found in south and southeast Asia. The butterfly belongs to the subgenus Chilasa, the black-bodied swallowtails.
Lucas called it Papilio dissimilis; the accepted name today is Chilasa clytia.

n102-1.name: Volta Swallowtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “This is a large species; all its wings are slightly toothed, brownish black above, and crossed in the middle by a fairly broad white band faintly tinged with yellow, a little fringed on the hindwings and cut by fine black veins. The small notches of the forewings are edged with faintly yellowish dots, those of the hindwings with oblong spots of the same colour.”

Papilio zenobia, the Zenobia swallowtail or Volta swallowtail, is a species of swallowtail butterfly from the genus Papilio that is found in Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, the Republic of the Congo and Uganda. It was first described by Johan…

n102-2.name: Mimetic Swallowtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “This species closely resembles Zenobius, but is much smaller and much less dark in colour. All the wings are toothed and finely edged with white on both surfaces; the forewings are reddish brown, crossed in the middle by a broad band finely cut by reddish veins and strongly interrupted towards the front.”

Papilio cynorta, the mimetic swallowtail or common white banded papilio, is a butterfly of the family Papilionidae. It is found in Africa, including Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, southern Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, the…

n112-1.name: Blue Albatross
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are nearly round, entire, of a frosted blue; the forewings have a black border, broadest at the apex and toothed inwardly near the base, and are lightly speckled with black, as are the veins. Beneath, the forewings are pearl grey, faintly yellow at the base, and near the base the hindwings carry silky, faintly bluish hairs.”

n112-2.name: Common Melwhite
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings above, and the forewings beneath, are white, both surfaces ending in a fairly broad black border, curved on the hindwings and forming on the forewings a long triangle whose point reaches the inner angle. Beneath, the costa of the forewings is edged with black and washed with a yellow that fades from the border towards the base.”
Melete lycimnia, the common melwhite, primrose flag or lycimnia white flag, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is found from Texas in the United States to Bolivia.

n114-1.name: Orange Albatross
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are bluish white above, with the hind margin, the vein tips and the costa of the forewings black. The black band, broadest at the apex, is lightly toothed inwardly; the middle of the hindwings is white and faintly orange where the marigold-coloured patch beneath shows through.”
Appias ada, the rare albatross, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found on the Moluccas, New Guinea, Indonesia, Australia and the Solomon Islands.
Melete lycimnia, the common melwhite, primrose flag or lycimnia white flag, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is found from Texas in the United States to Bolivia.

n114-3.name: Western Dotted Border
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are white. The forewings carry at the apex an arched and widened patch, sometimes elliptical, sometimes joined into a continuous band, and their base is orange with a blackish costa. Beneath, the apex is paler and faintly greenish, the base a deeper orange spreading much further than above.”
Mylothris poppea, the Poppea dotted border, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is found in Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana and Togo.

n116-1.name: Round-winged Vagrant
facts: Nepheronia pharis, the round-winged vagrant, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is found in Sierra Leone, Guinea, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, the Republic of the Congo, Angola, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the…
Lucas called it Pieris phaloe; the accepted name today is Nepheronia pharis.

n116-2.name: Yellow Albatross
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white faintly tinged with blue above, with a dark base. The forewings have the whole costa black and, at the tip, a border of the same colour, sinuous inwardly and widened at the apex, where it is divided by a broken band or by two white spots. Beneath, the hindwings are entirely pearl grey with a faint violet gleam.”

Appias paulina, known variously as the yellow albatross, lesser albatross, common albatross or Christmas Island white, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found from India to Samoa, including Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, New Caledonia, Thailand and Australia.

n116-3.name: Peak White
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above with a dark base. The male has at the tip of the forewings a black border, sinuous inwardly and broader at the apex, where it shows a transverse row of five or six white triangular spots pointing outward; the hindwings are edged by a run of closely set oval black spots.”
Pontia callidice, the lofty Bath white or peak white, is a small butterfly of the yellows and whites family (Pieridae), which occurs in the Palearctic realm.
Lucas called it Pieris calypso; the accepted name today is Pontia callidice.

n118-1.name: Caper White
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above, with a broad black hind border entirely divided by a row of white spots, the foremost oval, the rest round and smaller. The forewings also have, towards the middle of the costa, a curved transverse black band, broader in the female than in the male; beneath, the hindwings are strongly veined with black and marked with deep yellow.”

Belenois java, the caper white or common white, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae found in Australia, Indonesia, and Melanesia. It is highly migratory and is often confused with the cabbage white.

n118-2.name: Zebra White
facts: Pinacopteryx is a monotypic genus of pierid butterflies found in Africa containing Pinacopteryx eriphia, the zebra white.
Lucas called it Pieris eriphia; the accepted name today is Pinacopteryx eriphia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above in the male and yellow-tinged white in the female, with a black hind border sinuous on its inner side, very broad in the female. Both sexes are black beneath, with a very large orange patch at the base of the forewings and a transverse row of four or five oval greenish spots on the hind margin.”

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are white above, with the base and most of the costa ashen, the veins black and the middle one much widened, and at the tip a black border carrying four or five small oblong white spots. The hindwings above are a fine yellow, turning orange towards the anal angle, with the whole hind margin black.”

Lucas, 1835: “The male is white above, with the hind margin of the hindwings and two thirds of the costa of the forewings black, the forewings also bearing at the tip a very large triangular black space. Beneath, the forewings are black with a whitish crescent in the middle; the hindwings are ochre yellow, with a fairly broad black border saw-toothed on its inner side.”
Delias belisama is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It was described by Pieter Cramer in 1779.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is bluish white above, with a black apex divided transversely by an arched band of four or five oval white spots, and a narrow black border to the hindwings. The female is dull white above with each wing broadly edged in black; both sexes are black beneath, with about the front third of all four wings yellow and pricked with blackish.”

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are white above with a black apex divided transversely by an arched band of four or five white spots; the hindwings are faintly bluish above with a fairly broad black border cut by a run of whitish dots. Beneath, the hindwings are clouded yellow from base to middle, then black to the tip, with a marginal row of six marigold-coloured spots, three heart-shaped and three nearly round.”
Delias isse is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It was described by Pieter Cramer in 1775.

n130-3.name: Indian Jezebel
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the male is bluish white with black veins, more pronounced on the forewings than the hindwings, and each wing ends in a broad black border faintly fringed with whitish, arched and gently sinuous inwardly. Along its whole length this border is divided by a row of fairly large oval spots, white on the forewings and faintly flesh-coloured on the hindwings.”

Delias eucharis, the common Jezebel, is a medium-sized pierid butterfly found in many areas of south and southeast Asia, especially in the non-arid regions of India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Myanmar and Thailand. The common Jezebel is one of the most common of the approximately 225…

n132-1.name: Painted Jezebel
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is a slightly bluish white above, with the hind margin of the hindwings black. The forewings end in a black band forming a long triangle, its inner side sinuous, cut along its length by a run of six whitish spots, the first five elliptical and larger, the sixth rounded. All four wings are entirely veined with black beneath.”
Delias hyparete, the painted Jezebel, is a medium-sized butterfly of the family Pieridae, found in South Asia and Southeast Asia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above, especially in the male. The forewings have the costa lightly edged with black and, at the tip, a large deep black triangular space, arched and faintly sinuous inwardly, divided opposite the apex by a transverse line of three or four small white spots. Both sexes are brownish black beneath, dusted with white, with a deep yellow oblique band at the apex of the forewings.”

n132-3.name: Imperial Jezebel
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above, broadly edged with black at their tips. The forewings carry at the apex an arched, spotted white band; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, both are velvet black with a whitish lunule in the middle, and the hindwings are crossed by a vermilion red band, spotted and winding, from the front edge to the inner edge.”
Delias harpalyce, the imperial white, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is endemic to Australia.

n134-1.name: wood white butterfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above with a very broad black hind border on which are ranged round spots close to the ground colour. Below the costa of the forewings, near this border, the male has a black space divided across by a white lunule; in the female this space merges with the border and shows, besides the lunule, an angular white band facing the apex.”
Delias aganippe, the wood white or red-spotted Jezebel, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae.

n134-2.name: Chiapas White
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are white, with a light black border at the tip of the hindwings and along the costa of the forewings, which carry at the apex a triangular black space whose point rests on the middle of the hind edge. Beneath, the hindwings are brownish black with two transverse bands, the front one pale sulphur yellow, the hind one white washed with yellow, separated by a streak of marigold red.”

Perrhybris pamela, the Pamela, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found from Mexico, Honduras, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama, south to Colombia, Venezuela, Suriname, French Guiana, Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia.

n134-3.name: Large Vagrant
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings above are white faintly tinged with green. The forewings are edged at the tip by a very black band of moderate width forming a long triangle pointing downward, its inner side sinuous and cut by five or six small longitudinal black strokes; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, the black of the costa and tip is replaced by pale ochre yellow.”
Nepheronia argia, the large vagrant, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found throughout Africa.

n144-1.name: West Virginia White
facts: Pieris virginiensis, the West Virginia white, is a butterfly found in North America in the Great Lakes states, along the Appalachians from New England to Alabama, and in southern Ontario. They are often found in moist deciduous forests.

n144-2.name: Common Wanderer?
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is greenish white above with the veins and the hind margin black; the costa of the forewings is likewise black, and their tip shows a marginal row of whitish dots. In the female these dots appear on all four wings, the ground is less green and the veins are wider. Beneath, the hindwings are pearl grey with a faint violet gleam.”

Pareronia valeria, the common wanderer or Malayan wanderer, is a medium-sized butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites, and is found in India and Southeast Asia. The butterfly found in India is sometimes considered as a separate species, Pareronia hippia.

n144-3.name: Banded Patch
facts: Chlosyne endeis, known generally as the banded checkerspot or banded patch, is a species of crescents, checkerspots, anglewings, etc. in the butterfly family Nymphalidae.

n146-1.name: Black-spotted White
facts: Leptosia nina, the psyche, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae and is found in Indian subcontinent, southeast Asia and Australia. The upper forewing has a black spot on a mainly white background.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a cheerful tawny above, with the veins black and widened; the hind margin is also black, with two rows of unequal white dots preceded outwardly by a small broken edging of the same colour. The forewings have at the apex a large triangular black space crossed obliquely by a fine white angular band made up of five touching spots.”
Hebomoia leucippe is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is endemic to the Moluccas and Peleng in Indonesia.

n146-3.name: Great Orange Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings above are a vivid tawny, lightly glazed with red, with a clouded greenish-yellow base and the veins and whole outer edge black; parallel to the hind edge runs a row of black triangular spots pointing towards the base, larger and closer in the female. The hindwings are a fine lemon yellow above, edged in the female by a black band toothed inwardly.”
Hebomoia glaucippe, the great orange-tip, is a butterfly belonging to the family Pieridae, that is the yellows and whites. It is found in the Indomalayan realm and Wallacea.

n148-1.name: White Orange Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is bluish white above, the female yellowish white. In both sexes the forewings carry at the tip a very large triangular black space bearing a broad, arched patch of dawn orange, a little paler in the female and cut by a transverse line of black dots. The hindwings have the hind margin black in both sexes and the edge slightly sinuous.”
Ixias marianne, the white orange tip, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, found in India and Sri Lanka.

n148-2.name: Yellow Orange Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Both sexes are lemon yellow above. The forewings have at the tip a very large triangular black space on which sits an arched patch of dawn orange, narrowed at its lower end and a little paler in the female; the hindwings have a black hind margin. Beneath, all four wings are greenish yellow with usually only a very small blackish dot in the middle of each.”
Ixias pyrene, the yellow orange tip, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites, which is found in Sri Lanka, India and southeast Asia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are lemon yellow above, with the margin of the hindwings and the rear half of the forewings black. The forewings also carry, opposite the apex, an oblique transverse band, yellow or pale dawn according to sex, sinuous on both sides and marked with a dot near its lower end. This species is found in China, in Bengal and in the island of Java.”

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings above are faintly ashen at the base, lemon yellow along the inner edge and black over the rest, with a very large patch of dawn orange rounded outwardly, marked with a black dot in its middle and divided by veins of that colour. The hindwings are lemon yellow above with a black border, sometimes very narrow, sometimes fairly broad, toothed on its inner side.”

n150-2.name: Large Salmon Arab
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are pale tawny above with a row of black dots along the hind edge. The forewings have a black dot in the middle and, between this and the marginal dots, a curved, broken transverse black streak that does not reach the inner edge. Beneath, the hindwings are very pale yellow with a faintly blackish waved streak continuing the streak of the forewings.”

Colotis fausta, the large salmon Arab, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites, which is found in Israel, Syria, Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, India, Arabia, Chad, Somalia and United Arab Emirates.

n150-3.name: Three Spot Crimson Tip
facts: Colotis eunoma, the three spot crimson tip, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is found in Mozambique, Tanzania, and Kenya.

n150-4.name: Crimson Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white above. The forewings have at the tip a triangular black space almost entirely filled by a patch of fine carmine red; the hindwings carry a run of black triangular spots along the hind edge. Beneath, the apex of the forewings is whitish with a narrow reddish band cut lengthwise by a line of black dots.”
Colotis danae, the crimson tip or scarlet tip, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites. It is found in Asia and Africa.

n160-1.name: Round-winged Orange Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white above with a faintly dark base. The forewings have at the apex a fairly large triangular black space bearing a patch of vivid tawny, rounded outwardly, sinuous inwardly and a little narrowed at its lower end, and a very small black dot in the middle. The hindwings carry on the hind margin a row of nearly round black spots.”
Colotis euippe is a butterfly of the family Pieridae that is found in the Afrotropical realm.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white faintly tinged with yellow above, with a black base. The forewings have the apex black with a pale tawny patch rounded outwardly and deeply cleft, and a black dot in the middle, more or less distinct. The hindwings are broadly edged with black at the tip, with a broken row of fairly large white dots.”

n160-4.name: Purple Tip
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white, the base speckled with blackish. The forewings have at the tip an arched black border, narrow towards the inner angle and broad opposite the apex, where it is divided obliquely by a fine and very brilliant violet band, rounded outwardly; in the middle is a very black dot that repeats on the underside.”
Colotis ione, the bushveld purple tip, common purple tip, or violet tip, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. It is found in the dry parts of Africa south of the Sahara.

n162-1.name: Tailed Orange
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are canary yellow with a black border fringed with whitish outwardly, faintly sinuous inwardly and ending in a point at the inner angle; in the male the costa is also broadly edged with black, and from the base runs a straight black line along almost the whole lower edge, which is orange. The hindwings are white above with a black border finely and irregularly toothed towards the base.”
Eurema proterpia, the tailed orange, is a North and South American butterfly in the family Pieridae.

n162-2.name: Common Grass Yellow
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is a fine yellow. The forewings have at the tip a black border lightly edged with yellow outwardly and very sinuous inwardly, beginning in a point towards the middle of the costa and ending at the inner angle in a very broad hook; the hindwings have a narrower black border, arched and crenellated only on the side facing the base.”

Eurema hecabe, the common grass yellow, is a small pierid butterfly species found in Asia, Africa and Australia. They are found flying close to the ground and are found in open grass and scrub habitats.
Lucas called it Terias hecabe; the accepted name today is Eurema hecabe.

n162-3.name: Small Grass Yellow
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a fine deep yellow above, with a broad black border embracing their outline, a little narrower on the costa of the hindwings. Beneath, the border is a less deep black; the antennae are black, the body blackish above and yellow beneath, with a blackish line along the sides reaching the anal part. Found in the island of Amboina.”

Eurema brigitta, the small grass yellow or broad-bordered grass yellow, is a small butterfly of the family Pieridae, that is, the yellows and whites. It is found in India, other parts of Asia, Australia and Africa.
Lucas called it Terias candida; the accepted name today is Eurema brigitta.

n162-4.name: Sleepy Orange
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a vivid tawny above with a fairly broad black border, sinuous below, narrowed in the middle on the forewings and widened on the hindwings. The forewings also carry a black crescent in the middle. Beneath, the wings are paler and the border is replaced by blackish atoms; the hindwings are yellow with several rust-coloured spots.”

Eurema nicippe, the sleepy orange, is a North American butterfly in the family Pieridae. Its range spans from Central America to north along the United States–Mexico border, and it often travels further to non-mountainous regions of the Southeastern United States.

n164-1.name: Banded Yellow
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above, with a broad transverse band of blood red across the disc, cleft at each end and not reaching the tip of the hindwings. On the forewings this band is preceded outwardly by a narrower white band of five touching spots, and near the hind edge of each wing runs a line of white dots.”

n164-2.name: small grass yellow
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is a fine yellow above, the female a pale sulphur yellow, with a brownish-black border edged with reddish outwardly and sinuous inwardly, very narrow on the hindwings of the male and formed, on those of the female, by a run of spots of which the foremost is much the largest. Beneath, the forewings are yellow with a black dot in the middle.”
Eurema smilax, the small grass yellow, is a small pierid butterfly species found in Australia, with some additional records from India, Indonesia and Niger.

n164-3.name: Topaz Arab
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of the wings is a shining silvery green, ending on the forewings in a large triangular space of dark green and on the hindwings in a clouded band carrying a row of black dots. Beneath, all four wings are meadow green with a few rusty spots in the middle and light silvery shades along the inner edge. Found on the west coast of Africa.”
Colotis amata, the Small Salmon Arab, is a small butterfly in the family Pieridae. It is primarily found in South Asia in countries like India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

n164-4.name: Clouded Sulphur
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are canary yellow above, with a fairly broad black border divided, on the forewings of the female, by a strongly interrupted yellow spotted band. The forewings have an oblong black dot towards the middle of the costa; the hindwings have a pale, rounded orange patch on the disc, and beneath two silver dots, the outer one smaller.”
Colias philodice, the common sulphur or clouded sulphur, is a North American butterfly in the family Pieridae, subfamily Coliadinae.

n164-5.name: Southern Dogface
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are a fine yellow above. The forewings, whose apex is a little sharp, have the front half of the costa dark, a fairly large black dot in the middle, and at the tip a very broad black border whose inner side is sinuous and deeply notched in the middle, its outer side finely cut with yellow and red-brown. The hindwings are rounded and marked in the middle with two orange dots.”
Zerene cesonia, the southern dogface, is a North and South American butterfly in the family Pieridae, subfamily Coliadinae.

n174-1.name: Orange Migrant
facts: Catopsilia scylla, the orange migrant or orange emigrant, is a species of butterfly that lives in South East Asia and Australasia. Its larvae feed predominantly on plants of the genera Cassia and Senna.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining greenish white; the forewings are lightly edged with black, and the lemon yellow of the upperside reaches the middle of the forewings and the margin of the hindwings. All four wings are greenish beneath; the body is greenish white, the antennae black with a whitish club.”

n174-3.name: Apricot Sulphur
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are an orange yellow, a little shot with colour, above. Beneath, they are a deep ochre yellow, with silvery discal dots and winding reddish lines accompanied by a multitude of rusty atoms; in some individuals the silver dots have little brilliance. This species is found in Guiana and Brazil.”
Phoebis argante, the apricot sulphur or Argante giant sulphur, is a butterfly in the family Pieridae.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is a fine lemon yellow, a little matt towards the tip. Beneath, they are greenish or greyish and shining, with a rusty line running from the apex of the forewings towards the middle of the inner edge of the hindwings. The body is lemon yellow above and faintly yellowish white beneath.”

n176-2.name: Orange-barred Sulphur
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a vivid lemon yellow, a little matt towards the tip, and almost rounded in shape. The forewings have towards the middle a transverse orange patch of varying size; the hindwings are orange, sometimes from the middle to the tip, sometimes only at the tip, and the hind edge of both is cut by very small black dots.”
Phoebis philea, the orange-barred sulphur, is a species of butterfly found in the Americas including the Caribbean.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are entire and greenish white. The upperside of the forewings shows at the slightly pointed apex a fine triangular patch of dawn orange running from the middle of the costa to the middle of the hind edge, bordered outwardly by a black line and marked on its inner side by a large black dot. Beneath, all the wings are greenish white with a rusty, faintly purplish patch near the centre.”

n178-2.name: White Angled-Sulphur
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are greenish white above with a central orange dot having a black pupil. The forewings also carry, towards the middle of the costa, a large patch of lemon yellow. Beneath, the wings are greenish and faintly netted, with a flesh-coloured central dot answering the eye-spot of the opposite surface.”
Anteos clorinde, the white angled-sulphur or the ghost brimstone, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae. The species was originally described by Jean-Baptiste Godart in 1824.

n180-1.name: Gnidus Metalmark
facts: Lucas, 1835: “In the male the wings are white on both surfaces, with the base tawny and the tip black; the tip of the forewings shows above a run of small white strokes. Beneath, the hindwings carry towards the hind edge some twenty silver spots, the three at each end elongated on a white ground, the others round on a rusty ground, all edged with black.”
Helicopis gnidus, the gnidus metalmark or spider-wing cupid, is a species of butterfly in the family Riodinidae.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with an orange band, more or less narrow. On the forewings the band descends obliquely from the middle of the costa to the inner angle, where it bends a little; on the hindwings it is arched outwardly and runs from the apex to the anal angle, near which is an oblong red dot. Beneath, the space between base and band shows a multitude of small pale ochre dots.”

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining carmine red, with the outer margin and the costa of the forewings black. The black of the costa shows three unequal teeth above and reaches beyond the middle of the surface beneath; the hindwings often have a small black lunule at their centre. The body is red above and yellowish beneath.”
Lucas called it Myrina jafra; the accepted name today is Cheritra jafra.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a greenish violet blue, changing to violet, with the whole costa and the apex of the forewings black. Beneath, they are lilac or pale shining violet, with seven or eight black dots ringed with whitish scattered over the middle of each wing; the anal region of the hindwings is greenish blue with two short white bands. The tails are black tipped with white.”

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining cornflower blue above with a black apex; the forewings of the male have a greyish eye-spot towards the middle of the costa. Beneath, they are dark brown with the origin of the costa red on all four wings; the hindwings carry a white, waved, broken transverse line edged with black on its inner side, and two black eye-spots. Found in Guiana and Brazil.”

Lucas, 1835: “In the male the wings are a shining cornflower blue above, in the female a pale violet blue, with the apex of the forewings and the outer edge of the hindwings brownish black. Both sexes are a whitish satin grey beneath with a waved line of small black arcs, and the hindwings have at the anal angle two black eyes with a tawny iris, separated by a cluster of silvery blue atoms. This species is found in Bengal.”

n182-4.name: Dull Oakblue
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is a deep velvet violet above, with the channel of the hindwings blackish. Beneath, the wings are blackish brown netted with grey, with a run of three golden-green rings on the middle of the forewings and a small band of atoms of the same green at the anal angle of the hindwings, ending in a large black dot. The tail is black with a white tip.”
Arhopala centaurus, the centaur oakblue or dull oakblue, is a species of lycaenid or blue butterfly found in India and southeast Asia to the Philippines.
Lucas called it Polyommatus helus; the accepted name today is Arhopala centaurus.
Euploea eunice, commonly called the blue-banded king crow, is a species of butterfly that belongs to the Danaid group of the brush-footed butterflies family. It is found in the Indomalayan realm.

n184-2.name: Blue-spotted Jewel Moth
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are velvet black above, with a shot gleam from violet blue to azure according to the light; their front half is unspotted, the rest carries a great many white dots, the outer ones smaller and ranged along the edge. The hindwings above are brownish black, matt ash grey towards the apex; beneath, they show a dozen small violet spots between the middle and the apex.”

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are black on both surfaces and crossed between the middle and the tip by a fairly broad white band, sinuous on its sides and cut by fine veins of the ground colour, preceded outwardly by one or two white dots and inwardly by four or five more. The hindwings above are brownish black with a white patch set transversely at the base.”
Amauris niavius, the friar, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in the forests of tropical Africa.

n194-2.name: Monarch
facts: The monarch butterfly or simply monarch is a milkweed butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. Other common names, depending on region, include milkweed, common tiger, wanderer, and black-veined brown.

Lucas, 1835: “The ground of the forewings is black, and at the base is a large longitudinal tawny patch divided unequally in three by a forked black vein; opposite the apex is a white, spotted transverse band preceded outwardly by two marginal lines of white dots. The hindwings are brownish black with two rows of white dots on the hind margin and eight longitudinal white streaks running to the base.”

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above and dark brown beneath. The forewings carry on their front half three longitudinal spots of shining greenish yellow, two converging at the base and enclosing the third, which is much shorter; opposite the apex is a transparent transverse band faintly tinged with yellow, followed by white dots in two lines parallel to the hind edge.”

n198-1.name: Linnaeus Tree Nymph
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are elliptical, entire and a little transparent. Their upperside is greyish white with black veins and a black hind border, fairly broad, very sinuous on its inner side and divided across its whole width, at least on the forewings, by a run of large white dots, some round, some oval; between each vein, towards the tip, is a black lance-shaped spot reaching the border.”

Idea idea, also known as Linnaeus's idea or rice paper, is a large butterfly that belongs to the danaid group of the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1763 Centuria Insectorum.
Lucas called it Idea agelia; the accepted name today is Idea idea.

n200-1.name: Sara Longwing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are deep black above with a blue gleam at the base. The forewings have two oblique transverse patches of sulphur yellow, one in the middle and one near the apex, the latter very narrow and made of four touching spots; the hindwings are unspotted above, their hind edge a little toothed and finely edged with white at the notches.”

The Sara longwing is a species of neotropical heliconiid butterfly found from Mexico to the Amazon Basin and southern Brazil. It is a colourful species: the dorsal wing surface is black with a large medial patch of metallic blue that is framed by two bands of white on the forewings.

n200-2.name: Postman Butterfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are a fairly deep black above. The forewings carry in the middle a broad transverse band of dull minium red, a little oblique, ending almost in a point below and more sinuous in the female than in the male; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, the hindwings are brownish black with the front half of the costa dull sulphur yellow and a few blood-red dots ranged in a half circle against the base.”

Heliconius melpomene, the postman butterfly, common postman or simply postman, is a brightly colored, geographically variable butterfly species found throughout Central and South America. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.

Lucas, 1835: “Between the middle and the apex the forewings carry a broad transverse band of more or less vivid vermilion red starting from the costa, with a single tooth outwardly near its lower end and not reaching the inner edge; at the base is a longitudinal yellow line ending in a dot. The hindwings have near their origin a straight band of sulphur yellow of moderate width.”

n202-1.name: Zebra Long Wing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are black with bands of sulphur yellow. The forewings have three, the two outer ones transverse and oblique, the inner running straight from the base to the middle of the surface, where it bends a little to reach the hind edge; the hindwings have two transverse bands, the upper broad, straight and continuous, the lower curved and made of dots.”

Heliconius charithonia, the zebra longwing or zebra heliconian, is a species of butterfly belonging to the subfamily Heliconiinae of the family Nymphalidae. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1767 12th edition of Systema Naturae.

n202-2.name: Clearwing Mimic-Queen
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are deep black with three faintly yellowish, transparent bands; the triangular patch at the base is the largest, while the transverse band across the middle is narrower and divided into five spots, the three lower ones dot-like. The hindwings are faintly yellowish and transparent, with widened veins and a black hind border, and four or five curved teeth.”
Lycorea ilione, the clearwing mimic queen is a species of nymphalid butterfly in the subfamily Danainae. The species was first described by Pieter Cramer in 1775.

n202-3.name: Lysimnia Tigerwing
facts: Mechanitis lysimnia, the confused tigerwing, sweet-oil tiger or lysimnia tigerwing, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Johan Christian Fabricius in 1793.
Lucas called it Heliconia narcea; the accepted name today is Mechanitis lysimnia.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is faintly yellowish. The forewings have at the apex a triangular black space on which sits a patch of fine pale tawny, rounded outwardly, sinuous inwardly and narrowed at its lower end; the hindwings carry a row of well-spaced black spots on the hind margin. The body is whitish beneath and black above.”
Acraea egina, the elegant acraea, is a species of butterfly in the family Nymphalidae with an extensive range in sub-Saharan Africa.
Lucas called it Acraea zidora; the accepted name today is Acraea egina.

Lucas, 1835: “In this species the wings are proportionally less narrow than in the preceding ones. Their upperside is a deep matt black with the hind edge cut by white and slightly sinuous. The forewings are crossed by two lines of faintly shining sulphur-yellow spots, the inner line of about six spots arching from the middle of the costa towards the inner angle, the outer of four spots midway to the apex.”

Bematistes alcinoe, the alcinoe bematistes, is a species of butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, São Tomé and Príncipe, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia,…

n214-1.name: Acting Heliconian
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of the hindwings is dark brown at the base and along the hind edge, and crossed between these by a broad curved band of tawny or cherry red, toothed outwardly and marked in the middle with a few black dots; in the male this band just reaches the forewings, in the female it rises much higher and is divided into five oval spots.”

n214-2.name: Flame
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are blackish brown and crossed by a band, reddish white in the male and very white in the female, broader in her than in him, sinuous on its sides and cut by fine veins of the ground colour; it descends obliquely from the costa towards the hind angle, narrows greatly above it and folds inward to reach the inner edge. The hindwings are reddish in the male and reddish white in the female.”

Dryas iulia, commonly called the Julia butterfly, Julia heliconian, the flame, or flambeau, is a species of brush-footed butterfly. The sole representative of its genus Dryas, it is native from Brazil to southern Texas and Florida, and in summer can sometimes be found as far north as eastern…

n214-3.name: Juno Silverspot
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are dark brown with ochre-yellow spots arranged thus: two longitudinal at the base, the front one shorter; two nearly round in the middle; five oblong, unequal and touching, forming a transverse band opposite the apex. The hindwings above are rust-coloured with rays or streaks and a dark brown marginal band.”

Dione juno, the Juno silverspot, juno longwing, or Juno heliconian, is a species of butterfly of the subfamily Heliconiinae in the family Nymphalidae found from southern United States to South America.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are black above, with the inner edge and two bands tawny: the front band runs from the base to about the middle of the surface, where it is deeply cleft, then descends curving and widening to near the anal angle; the outer band lies obliquely opposite the apex without reaching the edges. The hindwings are tawny above with black streaks and a broad, curved, crenellated black border.”

Lucas, 1835: “The male is a vivid tawny above; the female a light tawny, a little darkened towards the base of the forewings. These have a black, slightly concave hind edge, and their apex shows from that edge to the middle of the costa a large triangular black space mostly filled by an oblique tawny patch cleft behind. The hindwings are toothed and end in a fairly broad black border divided by a double row of dusky tawny spots.”

n226-1.name: Dido Longwing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are toothed and black above. The forewings have two bands of celadon green, one longitudinal, one transverse: the first, from the base, is lance-shaped and reaches the disc, keeping nearer the front edge than the inner; the second, broader and strongly interrupted, is made of five unequal oblong spots, and the costa carries a line of three or four small whitish-green spots from its middle to the apex.”

Philaethria dido, the scarce bamboo page or dido longwing, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Central America and tropical South America, both east and west of the Andes, from Brazil and Ecuador northwards to Mexico.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are nearly round and toothed. Their upperside is velvet black with a violet gleam, and a broad terminal band of ochre yellow, repeated beneath, formed of closely set wedge-shaped spots. Beneath, each wing is rust-coloured and drawn thus: between base and middle, three transverse bands of greyish green cut lengthwise by black lines, then a series of small spots parallel to the terminal band.”

n228-1.name: Orange Lacewing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are tawny above with a blackish terminal band divided by a run of whitish crescents concave outwardly. Opposite the apex of the forewings is a large triangular space of bluish black joined to the border, carrying an oblique, sinuous white transverse band separated from the crescents by an arc of four or five white dots. The border of the hindwings is preceded inwardly by two rows of black spots.”
Cethosia penthesilea, the orange lacewing, is a species of heliconiine butterfly found in Southeast Asia, as well as the Australia's Northern Territory.

n228-2.name: Red Lacewing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are finely toothed and edged with whitish at the notches. The upperside is a vivid tawny in the male, a dark and faintly greenish brick colour in the female, with a very broad brownish-black border arched inwardly. This border casts a faint violet gleam and is entirely divided by two curved parallel lines of white crescents facing one another by their convex sides.”
Cethosia cydippe, the eastern red lacewing, is a species of butterfly from Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands. The Australian subspecies, C.

n230-1.name: Regal Fritillary
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are tawny above with about fifteen black spots: the foremost linear and set transversely beneath the costa, which is itself black; the next forming a zigzag transverse band across the middle; the rest round, smaller and ranged in a line parallel to the hind edge, which is covered by a fairly broad black band toothed inwardly and divided in the male by tawny lunules, in the female by white dots.”

The regal fritillary is a striking nymphalid butterfly found in tallgrass and mixed-grass prairies in the east-central United States. This prairie-specialist butterfly is deep orange with distinctive dark hindwings with two bands of spots.
Lucas called it Argynnis idalia; the accepted name today is Speyeria idalia.

n230-2.name: Indian Fritillary
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are yellowish tawny strewn with black spots above and end in a black border crenellated inwardly and carrying two rows of bluish lunules facing one another. Opposite the apex of the forewings is a large triangular bluish-black space crossed by an oblique, sinuous white band cut by the veins and marked below with two black dots. Daubenton called it the Leopard of China.”
The Indian fritillary is a species of butterfly of the nymphalid or brush-footed family. It is usually found from south and southeast Asia to Australia.
Lucas called it Argynnis niphe; the accepted name today is Argyreus hyperbius.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are dark brown above with a broad transverse band of greenish white set between the middle and the hind margin. On the forewings the band is a double row of spots, the inner ones smaller and crescent-shaped, the outer oval and each charged with a large black dot; on the hindwings it is continuous, preceded outwardly by a string of lunules, with two black eye-spots having a bluish pupil and a yellow iris.”

n234-1.name: Red Peacock
facts: Anartia amathea, the brown peacock, is a species of nymphalid butterfly, found primarily in South America. This butterfly is very similar to the banded peacock or Anartia fatima, which primarily exists north of the range of Anartia amathea.

n234-2.name: blue admiral
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are greenish black above, a little shot, and crossed in the middle and towards the tip by a pale arched blue band, divided on the hindwings by a line of black dots. Beneath, the male is dark black from the base to beyond the middle, then wood grey strongly waved with brown, with a sinuous, almost marginal line of ashen atoms and a dirty white dot on the disc of the hindwings. Found in China.”
Kaniska canace, the blue admiral, is a nymphalid butterfly, the only species of the genus Kaniska. It is found in south and southeast Asia.
Lucas called it Vanessa charonia; the accepted name today is Vanessa canace.

n234-3.name: Grey Pansy
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are ash-coloured, a little reddish in the male, with three blackish, waved transverse lines towards the rear, between which runs a transverse row of eye-spots, six on the forewings and five on the hindwings, all but the two middle ones having the inner side of the pupil tawny; there are also some blackish waves near the origin of the front edge of the forewings.”
Junonia atlites, the grey pansy, is a species of nymphalid butterfly found in South Asia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are tawny above with a dark base and a curved, transverse hind row of six violet dots edged with black, much larger on the hindwings, whose middle shows a small black spot; the forewings have beneath the costa three short, parallel, slightly arched transverse bands of the same colour. Beneath, the wings are like the upperside but generally paler and a little pricked with blackish. Inhabits the Cape of Good…”

n244-3.name: Golden Pansy
facts: Lucas, 1835: “This species differs from the one just described in that the origin of the costa of the forewings is brown instead of whitish; the eye at their inner angle is much larger and less round, flanked by two black dots inside the same iris; the upperside of the hindwings has no blue band but three lilac eyes, the front one larger and furnished with three white pupils.”

Junonia chorimene, the golden pansy, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Senegal, the Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Mali, Sierra Leone, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Ethiopia, Uganda, northern and western…

n246-1.name: Eyed Pansy
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings above are a deep velvet black in the male and brownish black in the female, with two black eyes having violet-blue pupils and a reddish-tawny iris. The forewings, whose costa is whitish from its origin to the middle, have near the base four small oblique lines alternately tawny and bluish, and towards the tip three white streaks, the innermost broader and shorter.”

Junonia orithya is a nymphalid butterfly with many subspecies occurring from Africa, through South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Australia. In India, its common English name is the blue pansy, but in southern Africa it is known as the eyed pansy as the name blue pansy refers to Junonia oenone.

n246-2.name: Dark Blue Pansy
facts: Junonia oenone, the blue pansy or dark blue pansy, is a Nymphalid butterfly native to Africa. "Blue pansy" is also used in India to describe Junonia orithya.

n246-3.name: Dark Blue Pansy
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are yellow inclining to tawny above, with all the edges black. This colour spreads broadly at the base of the hindwings and sets off a patch of violet or lapis blue, of much the same shape and size as in the preceding species. The forewings have at the apex, where the black widens entirely, two transverse yellowish streaks, the inner one shorter.”
Junonia oenone, the blue pansy or dark blue pansy, is a Nymphalid butterfly native to Africa. "Blue pansy" is also used in India to describe Junonia orithya.

n248-1.name: Mangrove Buckeye
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of each wing is dark brown with two black eyes, their pupil bluish and their iris yellowish grey. These eyes are immediately preceded outwardly by a tawny line, more or less deep, itself preceded by a double waved marginal line of the same grey as the iris. The forewings have towards the origin of the costa two small tawny streaks edged with black, and between the two eyes an oblique band, sometimes…”

Junonia evarete, the tropical buckeye or South American tropical buckeye, is a South American butterfly of the nymphalid (Nymphalidae) family. It has characteristic eye spots on the wings, which have a wingspan between 4.5 and 6.5 cm.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are blackish brown with a violet gleam running from the base to beyond the disc. The forewings have seven or eight white dots, one cut in two near the middle of the costa, the others in two lines parallel to the hind edge. The hindwings are unspotted on both surfaces, but their underside, entirely glazed with violet, shows two dark, waved transverse lines.”

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown on both surfaces, the outer edge of the forewings less deep. Parallel to that edge the hindwings carry a broad, curved, spotted band of vivid vermilion red, finely notched on its sides; beneath it appears again, but rosy white and a little narrower, accompanied by four red dots, three near the base and one towards the middle of the costa.”

n250-1.name: Tawny Rajah
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are brownish black above with a common, oblique tawny band across the disc. On the forewings the band is spotted, cleft in front and marked below the cleft with a line of three small black dots; on the hindwings it goes no further than the disc, and these wings have a reddish dot at the apex and a double row of unequal violet-blue dots along the outer edge.”

Charaxes bernardus, the tawny rajah, is a butterfly that belongs to the rajahs and nawabs group, that is, the Charaxinae group of the brush-footed butterflies family. This species can be found in India, China, Indomalaya, and onwards to Indonesia.
Lucas called it Nymphalis pollux; the accepted name today is Charaxes bernardus.

n250-2.name: Common Blue Charaxes
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blue-black above with two transverse hind rows of light blue dots and a quite terminal row of earthy yellow lunules. Beneath, the ground of all four wings is a faintly shining greyish brown; towards the base are black, waved transverse strokes lightly edged with bluish, followed by a winding transverse series of yellowish dots.”

Charaxes tiridates, the common blue charaxes, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Senegal, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo,…

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above with a tawny or yellowish band towards the tip of the forewings and a white band towards the tip of the hindwings. The band of the forewings descends from the costa to the inner angle and is made of tawny dots in the male and of large wedge-shaped yellowish spots in the female. The marginal band of the hindwings is preceded by a band of ashen blue carrying a curved row of eight…”
Charaxes eurialus is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found on Ambon Island, Seram and Saparua in Indonesia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are brownish black above, with the front half of the hindwings and a large triangular space at the origin of the inner edge of the forewings a livid yellow. The forewings have nine round spots of the same yellow, two a little beyond the middle of the costa and seven ranged parallel to the hind edge; the hindwings have two rows of blue lunules, the marginal one ending at the anal angle in a tawny crescent.”
Charaxes (Polyura) pyrrhus is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.

n262-1.name: Silver-studded Leafwing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “In this species the tooth before the anal angle of the hindwings stands out more than the others, and in the female the end of the tail is shaped, so to speak, like a foot. The wings above are brownish black with a violet gleam, with a broad, sinuous band of pale ochre yellow descending from the middle of the costa to the inner angle of the forewings, which carry one or more dots of the same yellow at the apex.”
Hypna is a butterfly genus of the family Nymphalidae. It is monotypic, containing only Hypna clytemnestra, the jazzy leafwing, marbled leafwing or silver-studded leafwing.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above, crossed obliquely in the middle by a band of violet-tinged white, narrower on the forewings than the hindwings. The hindwings have the lower edge tawny from the anal angle to the tail inclusive, with five violet dots, the three outer ones edged with black. Beneath, all the wings are rusty brown with a few black, curved transverse lines edged with bluish at the base.”

Palla decius, the white-banded palla, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Senegal, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, the Republic of the Congo, the western part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Angola.

n264-1.name: Common Pearl Charaxes
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the front half of the wings is white, passing to yellowish towards the costa of the forewings; the other half is rusty, with two transverse rows of large tawny dots and an intermediate row of blackish dots on the forewings, and the reverse arrangement on the hindwings. Beneath, all the wings are the yellow of a dead leaf, with a few brown, waved transverse lines pricked with bluish near the base.”
Charaxes varanes, the pearl emperor, Karkloof emperor, or pearl charaxes, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae, found in Africa from Saudi Arabia to South Africa.

Charaxes mycerina, the mycerina untailed charaxes, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Equatorial Guinea.
Lucas called it Nymphalis mycerina; the accepted name today is Charaxes mycerina.

n266-1.name: Orion Cecropian
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are brownish black above with a longitudinal tawny band covering about the whole front third of the surface, then narrowing to end a little short of the hind edge; towards the tip of the front edge is an oval white spot set lengthwise. The hindwings are brownish black above with a dusky tawny edge. Beneath, all four wings are brown shaded with grey, with two darker transverse bands near the base.”
Historis odius, the orion cecropian, is a species of crescents, checkerspots, anglewings, etc. in the butterfly family Nymphalidae.
Lucas called it Nymphalis rogerii; the accepted name today is Siderone marthesia.

n268-2.name: Dido Longwing
facts: Philaethria dido, the scarce bamboo page or dido longwing, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Central America and tropical South America, both east and west of the Andes, from Brazil and Ecuador northwards to Mexico.

n270-1.name: Pointed Sister
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above with a common, oblique white band across the disc, rounded at its front end and sharp or nearly so at the other. Opposite the apex the forewings carry an orange spot, more or less round in the male and an inverted triangle in the female, always separate from the white band; at the anal angle the hindwings have a small tawny patch bearing two black dots.”
Adelpha iphiclus, the Iphiclus sister, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.

n270-2.name: Turquoise Emperor
facts: Doxocopa laurentia, the turquoise emperor or Cherubina emperor, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae, subfamily Apaturinae.

Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are blackish brown with a common, oblique white band across the disc, less divided on the hindwings than on the forewings. The forewings have towards the origin of the costa three transverse spots of rusty red framed in black and separated by bluish ash; the hindwings have at the anal angle a tawny patch marked with two black dots. Beneath, two rusty lines with a white line between them run parallel…”

n280-2.name: Blood-red Glider
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a vermilion red, a little shot, above, with an almost terminal row of black dots, faint on the forewings and joined on the hindwings by an angular black line. Beneath, all four wings are a light tan brown with black hieroglyphs at the base, a common oblique rusty line across the middle and dark chevrons topped with violet dots at the tip. The body is brown above and yellowish beneath.”
Cymothoe sangaris, the blood-red glider, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Central Africa.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above, with a common discal band whose inner side is mostly white and whose outer side is slate blue, spreading in rays to the hind edge. This edge carries white dots, the inner ones oblong and set in an arched line, the outer ones on the notches. Beneath, all four wings are dark brown with two rows of marginal dots as above and a band of violet-tinged white.”
Lucas called it Nymphalis amasia; the accepted name today is Anaea anassa.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of both sexes is a smoky black, crossed between the middle and the hind edge of the hindwings by a tawny band divided along its whole length by a curved row of seven very black oval spots, all, even the double and smaller anal one, carrying a blue dot in the middle. In the male this tawny band is narrower and surmounted by a large, faintly shining lilac patch. Daubenton called it the Palatine.”

n282-2.name: Great Eggfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is brownish black beneath, and shows towards the middle of each wing a white patch surrounded by a violet gleam and cut by the veins: round on the hindwings, oblong and oblique on the forewings, which carry a similar but much smaller patch at the apex. Lucas lists more than a dozen names under which earlier authors had described this variable species.”
Hypolimnas bolina, the great eggfly, common eggfly, varied eggfly, or in New Zealand the blue moon butterfly, is a species of nymphalid butterfly found from Madagascar to Asia and Australia.

n284-1.name: Blue-banded Eggfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are a shot black with a common, arched blue band across the disc, behind which run three strings of blue spots, the inner ones wedge-shaped, the outer lunulate and placed opposite the notches, which are edged with white on both surfaces. Beneath, the wings carry the same pattern, but the edge is brown, the band and spots bluish white, and the costa of the forewings is dotted and dusted with white…”
Hypolimnas alimena, the blue-banded eggfly, is a species of butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in the Solomon Islands, Indonesia, New Guinea and Australia.

n284-2.name: Blue Diadem Butterfly
facts: Hypolimnas salmacis, the blue diadem, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, São Tomé and Príncipe, the DRC, Uganda, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya and…

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are black above; the forewings show two transverse bands of a deep colour inclining to reddish, the one at the base very broad, the one nearer the front narrower and rounded on its outer side. The hindwings have a single band of the same colour, narrow, a little sinuous on the inner side and rounded behind. Beneath, the forewings also show a narrow, slightly arched yellow band and a very narrow blue…”

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a violet-blue gleam, changing in the male and absent in the female. In both sexes the forewings have at the base a longitudinal line, in the middle a transverse band and at the apex an oblique dash of a green that looks more or less golden according to the light; the hindwings have a band of golden or bluish green along the outer edge. Beneath, the forewings are carmine red from their…”
Pseudaletis clymenus, the common fantasy, is a butterfly in the family Lycaenidae. The species was first described by Hamilton Herbert Druce in 1885.

n286-4.name: Camberwell Beauty
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are velvet black above with a shining orange band across the disc, a little curved and scarcely rising beyond the centre of the forewings. Beneath, the forewings are a shining blackish brown with the rear half of the costa violet grey and the disc yellowish and furnished with black hairs lying flat; the hindwings are brown faintly shaded with grey, with an arched transverse line of a few blackish dots.…”

Nymphalis antiopa, known as the mourning cloak in North America and the Camberwell beauty in Britain, is a large butterfly native to Eurasia and North America. The immature form of this species is sometimes known as the spiny elm caterpillar.

n288-1.name: One-spotted Prepona
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a common, oblique band of shining greenish blue across the disc, arched and interrupted near the costa of the forewings and ending in a point on the hindwings. Beneath, the wings are brownish with three transverse bands of pearl grey, a black dot at the base of each wing and a waved line of the same colour descending from the front quarter of the costa to the inner angle.”
Archaeoprepona demophon, the one-spotted prepona, banded king shoemaker, or demophon shoemaker is a butterfly belonging to the family Nymphalidae.

Lucas, 1835: “Both sexes of Nymphalis Demophon closely resemble the female of Nymphalis Demodice on the upperside; but the male of the latter has the blue band surrounded by a broad violet gleam, ending in a point a little beyond the disc of the forewings instead of being interrupted and arched near their upper edge. Beneath, rather more than the front half of all four wings is greyish white.”
Prepona laertes, the shaded-blue leafwing or Laertes prepona, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in large parts of Central and South America.

n298-1.name: Beltrão’s Owl Butterfly
facts: One of the owl butterflies: the underside carries a huge eyespot that reads as an owl’s eye when the wings are closed.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a common band of shining violet blue across the disc, which reaches almost to the root of the wings while losing its brilliance. The forewings have towards the middle of the costa an oblique white spot and towards the tip white dots in one row in the male and two in the female; the hindwings, whose notches are also white, carry a series of red dots along the hind edge.”

n302-1.name: Menelaus Blue Morpho
facts: Another Trojan name from Linnaeus. The blue is structural: the scales are stacked like tiny Christmas trees and reflect only blue light.
The undersides are brown with eyespots, so a flying morpho seems to flash on and off.

n304-1.name: White Morpho
facts: A pale morpho whose white takes a faint pearly blue in the light. Named for Laertes, father of Odysseus.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings above are velvet black, especially towards the base, with faint, slightly yellowish notches. The forewings carry a transverse band of fine blue that shines according to the light, much broader towards the base and divided in three by the veins; near the outer edge a longitudinal band of pale yellow crossed by black veins runs from the apex of the forewings to the anal angle of the hindwings.”
Dasyophthalma rusina is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Brazil, from Bahia to Santa Catarina.
Lucas called it Pavonia lycaon; the accepted name today is Dasyophthalma rusina.

n306-2.name: coconut caterpillar
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are very entire and dark brown above. The forewings, whose front edge is strongly arched, are crossed from the middle of that edge by a curved, slightly sinuous tawny band reaching the inner angle and sometimes continuing, though shorter, to the corresponding angle of the hindwings; this band is more or less cleft at its origin. Beneath, all four wings are paler and finely pricked with grey, with a small…”
Brassolis sophorae, commonly known as the coconut caterpillar, is a species of large butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in South America.

Lucas, 1835: “In this species the forewings are entire and a little transparent. Their upperside is dark brown, sometimes unspotted, sometimes carrying parallel to the hind edge a run of four or five dots, the second from the costa black in a grey ring, the others wholly bluish. The hindwings are a little toothed and end outwardly in a small blunt tail; their rear half is deep black with some twenty blue spots, most charged with…”
Pierella lena, the Lena pierella, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Suriname, the Guianas, Peru, Bolivia and Brazil.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are a little transparent, dark brown on both surfaces, with a linear white band descending obliquely from the end of the costa to the end of the inner edge. The upperside of the hindwings has about the front half and the outer edge dark brown, and all the rest tawny or Spanish-tobacco coloured, with a very white band edged with blackish; between this band and the hind edge are two very black eyes with…”
Pierella nereis is a butterfly species from the subfamily Satyrinae in the family Nymphalidae. It was first described by Dru Drury in 1782 from Brazil.

n310-2.name: White-tailed Longtail
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The body is a dusky blackish with a tint of silky green at the upper root of the wings. The transverse white line of the forewings is made of four or five spots, touching or merely separated by veins, and ends a little before the inner angle; the hindwings have four more white, diaphanous but very small spots, one adjoining the hind edge of the streak near its middle and three in a little line near the costa.”
Cecropterus doryssus, commonly known as the white-tailed longtail, is a species of dicot skipper in the butterfly family Hesperiidae. It is found in Central America, North America, and South America.
Lucas called it Hesperia versicolor; the accepted name today is Mimoniades versicolor.
